PtMC 2022
Growth of four different crop species in
supplemented loamy lunar regolith
Ava Thorsen Solomon Debrezion Sabina Thabit-Yousef Sara Petollari
Image of White Buckwheat flowers grown in regolith 35 days after the start of the
experiment. Photo credit: Ava Thorsen, March 9, 2022
Abstract
The ability to grow food on celestial bodies is essential to the long-term missions
required for future space exploration. Due to the difficulty of transporting materials to
other planets, using available regolith for food growth is vital. Our experiment analyzed the
possibility of growing crops in lunar regolith that was modified to have a loamy texture and
imitate the properties of Earth soil. Four different crop species were grown in both
modified regolith and fertile earth soil for seven weeks. Fagopyrum esculentum
(buckwheat) plants had significantly greater biomass in lunar regolith than in earth soil. At
the same time, Triticum aestivum L. (wheat), Solanum lycopersicum (tomato), and Pisum
sativum (pea) crops showed no significant difference in overall biomass. Both regolith and

earth soil-grown crops produced flowers and fruits. Our results show that it is possible to
grow healthy crops in lunar regolith when modified to mimic specific attributes of fertile
Earth soil.
Introduction
Human colonization of the moon has long been a dreamed-about possibility for the
future. With new technology and scientific innovation, this dream can become a feasible
reality; however, efficient food accessibility presents a significant problem [1]. Current
astronauts rely heavily on dried, pre-made foods; however, these foods are not sustainable
for long-term missions due to nutrition and the expense of transporting them [1]. For
humans to live on celestial bodies such as the moon, it is vital that they are able to grow
food crops using materials readily available to them. The moon does not have soil, the
usual substrate for growing crops. It instead is covered by a layer of fine dust called lunar
regolith [2]. Lunar regolith is infertile and lacks many qualities essential for healthy plant
development [2].
Many studies have compared plant growth in simulated lunar regolith to plant
growth in both fertile and infertile earth soil. According to Wamelink et al. 2014, lunar
regolith simulant was less capable of producing plant growth than very infertile earth soil
[3]. These results show that crops cannot thrive in regolith alone, which introduces the
question of how regolith can be made more fertile. Wamelink et al. 2019 explored how the
addition of organic matter affected biomass production in lunar regolith [4]. Overall,
regolith with the addition of organic matter performed better than regolith without it;
however, the amount of biomass produced by modified regolith was far smaller than the
quantity of biomass produced by earth soil modified in the same way.
To effectively grow crops in regolith, more research needs to be done to figure out
ways to reduce the biomass production discrepancy between regolith and earth soil. The
goal of our research was to modify lunar regolith in a way that gives it properties of loamy
earth soil. Loamy earth soil is very fertile due to its balanced variety of particle sizes that
provide ideal moisture and nutrient retention [5]. Modifying lunar regolith to mimic fertile
earth soil would attempt to increase growth productivity by improving moisture retention,
nutrient availability, and aeration. Unlike the research method used by Wamelink et al. in
2014, we chose to use a fertile soil control because we aimed to gauge how modified
2

regolith compares to soil capable of ample crop production. Using this control would more
adequately determine regolith's ability or lack thereof to support human life. We
investigated whether Fagopyrum esculentum, Triticum aestivum L., Pisum sativum, and
Solanum lycopersicum were able to grow in modified lunar regolith. It was hypothesized
that loamy soil constructed with 52% regolith would be able to sustain seed and plant
development. If our findings support this hypothesis, effective crop production using lunar
regolith is conceivable.
Materials and Methods
2.1 Soils
LHS-1 Lunar Highlands Regolith simulant was used in this experiment. It was
purchased from Exolith Labs. Lunar regolith sampled from lunar highlands contains
specific minerals that can also be found in magmatic rocks on earth. The primary minerals
within the regolith simulant are anthorosite and glass-rich basalt [6]. The loamy earth soil
was gathered at 36.12432*N, 86.82381*W, which has a soil type classified as maury silt
loam [7]. The soil was collected at a 0-3 inch depth and had a high organic matter content.
No additives were combined with the earth soil at the time of planting.
The regolith was combined with many additives, each of which contributed to a trait
found in loamy earth soil. In order of concentration, the following materials were added to
the regolith. Specific percentages of each material used can be found in Table 1. Peat moss
increased the total porosity of the soil, allowing for better aeration and drainage.
Vermiculite served a similar purpose, improving drainage, aeration, and nutrient retention.
Compost was sourced from a residential anaerobic compost pile in planting zone 7a. It
added organic matter and nutrients to the regolith. The clay was sourced from 36.12386*N,
86.82377*W at a depth of seven feet. The smaller particles found in clay retain large
amounts of moisture and nutrients. GardenTone Vegetable fertilizer sourced from Epsoma
was used to increase the availability of usable nutrients, including Nitrogen and
Phosphorus. The earth soil, compost and clay additives were not sterile or free from seeds
and insects. At planting, the pH for both the earth soil control and the regolith mixture was
6.4. The pH of the regolith mixture was lowered using white vinegar.

2.2 Species Selection
Four species were chosen for this experiment, each from a different family. From
the Solanaceae family, Solanum lycopersicum or glacier tomato was selected. Pisum
sativum (iona pea) was selected from the Fabaceae family, Triticum aestivum L. (hard red
spring wheat) was selected from the Poaceae family, and Fagopyrum esculentum (common
buckwheat) was selected from the Polygonaceae family. These species were chosen due to
their yield ability, preferred climate, and hardiness. They all have the potential to produce a
good quantity of viable crops in a relatively short period, which is important in the context
of extraterrestrial farming. The hard red spring wheat seeds were sourced from All Good
Things Organic Seeds, the common buckwheat seeds were sourced from Baker Creek
Heirloom Seeds, and the two remaining seeds were sourced from Botanical Interests.
External bacteria may have been present on the seeds, as it was not eradicated.
2.3 Experimental Design
The growth portion of the experiment was conducted in an indoor environment, as
such conditions seemed the most likely to be present in an extraterrestrial mission. The
location was kept at a temperature of around 70 degrees. Plants were placed in front of an
east-facing window, from which they received bright, indirect light each day. Additionally,
light was supplemented by four 100w, full-spectrum, led grow lights for six hours each day.
Four plastic growing chambers were used to house the plants in this experiment.
The chambers included ventilating lids; however, the crops quickly outgrew them, and they
were removed after the first week. Each chamber had twelve individual units. Two
chambers were filled with the regolith mixture, and the remaining two were filled with
earth soil. One seed was planted per unit, and six seeds were planted per species in each
4

soil type. There were six replicants for each condition in this experiment. Figure 2 shows
the experimental setup, including where each seed was planted. The species and soil type
locations were not randomized, although the chambers were randomly rotated throughout
the experiment weekly to prevent location-related bias. The seeds were planted at the
depths recommended on their packages. Specific depths are detailed in table 2.
Figure 1. A visual representation of the growing set up of the growing set up.
The growing period lasted for seven weeks or 49 days. During this time, the plants
were watered regularly with reverse osmosis water. One chamber unit from each chamber
would be tested for moisture level using a moisture meter every weekday. The chamber
would be watered if the meter indicated that the soil was moist or dry. If the meter
indicated soil wetness, no water would be added for that day. On week two of the growing
period, all plants were fertilized with a water-soluble organic fertilizer.
Table 2. Shows the depth in which the seeds of each
plant were planted.
2.4 Measurements and Harvest
During the growing period, several measurements were taken each week. Plant
height data was gathered for each plant using a centimeter ruler. Leaf count was taken
each week, and it accounted for living leaves that had fully unfurled. Leaf count was not
taken for the wheat plants due to the difference in their structure. Starting on week four,
observations regarding the development of flowers were recorded for all plants. Flowering
was quantified by the presence of reproductive organs on a plant. Fruiting was recorded on
5

week seven of growth, and it was quantified by the presence of seeds or an encasing
intended to house future seeds. Each week photos were taken of all plants to document
development.
Each specimen was harvested from its growing chamber at the end of the seventh
week. Excess soil was removed from the roots, and each plant was dried, first in an oven for
approximately 1 hour at 60 degrees and then left in an open area for a week to ensure total
dryness. From the dried specimens, both above and below-ground weight was collected.
Results
The performance of the plants was measured in terms of germination rates, plant
height, leaf count, flowering rates, fruiting rates, and biomass. By the end of the growing
period, the regolith outperformed the earth soil in terms of total germination rate (Table 3).
There was no significant difference between the average heights of the plants during most
weeks of the growing period (Figure 2). Leaf count was significantly different only for the
buckwheat plants during the last two weeks (Figure 3). All species of plants except for
tomatoes flowered. This included eleven out of twelve buckwheat, five out of twelve peas,
and six out of twelve wheat plants. Two peas grown in lunar regolith produced fruits, and
three of the peas grown in earth soil fruited. One buckwheat plant and all wheat plants
were able to fruit in the earth soil, while none fruited in the regolith. No tomatoes
developed to the point of fruiting. In terms of total biomass, buckwheat growing in regolith
soil had a significantly higher biomass than the buckwheat growing in the earth soil.
Furthermore, the above-ground buckwheat biomass was significantly different between the
two soils (p < 0.01), as well as the below-ground biomass (p < 0.05). There was no significant
difference between the total biomasses of other plants (Figure 4).

chamber units for each type of plant. In total, the regolith was able to have a higher germination rate than the earth soil.

Discussion
Plants grown in modified lunar regolith performed similarly to, if not better, than
plants grown in fertile, loamy earth soil. The lack of statistical differences shows that crops
can grow in modified lunar regolith similarly to how they do in fertile earth soil. With more
testing, the solution of specific regolith modification has the potential to allow astronauts
to grow their own fresh food on the moon. The results found in previous research contrast
our findings. Wamelink et al. (3) and Wamelink et al. (4) reported significantly less plant
development in lunar soil than in the unfertile earth soil control. It is believed that our
results differ from past findings due to the specific additives combined with regolith. Such
additives increased overall nutrient availability and improved the soil texture which aided in
plant growth.
There were several limitations in this study, the most significant of which was water.
Due to the varying drainage rates of the soils, some periods of dryness occured. Another
8

important limitation to mention was container size. The plants quickly outgrew the growing
chambers, which may have altered growth patterns. Additionally, external seeds were not
eradicated before planting, and because of this, plants grew that were not intended as part
of the experiment. No data was collected on these plants; however, they may have affected
the growth of the plants in the same chamber unit. Future research addressing such
limitations and increasing the sample size and diversity would be beneficial. Furthermore,
an experiment designed to test different concentrations of regolith in the lunar regolith
mixture would expand upon our current findings and specify precisely how much additive
is needed for regolith to sustain viable crops.
In conclusion, Fagopyrum esculentum, Triticum aestivum L., Pisum sativum, and
Solanum lycopersicum crops were able to grow and thrive in a mixture containing 52%
lunar regolith. The data showed no significant disparity between the plants grown in
regolith compared to those grown in earth soil. This means that this regolith mixture has
the potential to effectively replace earth soil as a growing medium on extraterrestrial
bodies.
